citations.claim: The Rise, Litigation, and Collapse of the FTC Non-Compete Rule (2023–2026) 1.1 The Genesis and Scope of the 2024 FTC Rule Under the direction of former Chair Lina Khan, the Federal Trade Commission sought to fundamentally alter the national discourse on restrictive covenants by promulgating the 2024 Non-Compete Clause Rule
The rule was explicitly predicated on the economic theory that non-compete clauses keep wages artificially low, suppress new ideas, and rob the American economy of essential dynamism

The sweeping regulation sought to ban nearly all post-employment non-compete agreements nationwide, preempting all conflicting state laws and invalidating millions of existing agreements by declaring them an "unfair method of competition" under Section 5 of the FTC Act

Furthermore, the rule required employers to affirmatively rescind existing clauses and notify workers that their non-compete agreements were void, carving out only exceptionally narrow exceptions, such as for the bona fide sale of a business

Current Chairman Andrew N. Ferguson and Commissioner Melissa Holyoak dissented from the issuance of the rule, arguing that the FTC fundamentally lacked the statutory authority to issue substantive rules regarding unfair methods of competition
The dissenting commissioners articulated several core constitutional arguments against the agency's actions

The majority relied on Section 6(g) of the FTC Act as its source of authority, but the dissenters argued that Section 6(g) only authorizes procedural or internal operating rules, not substantive legal rules carrying the force of law

They also rejected the rule under the major questions doctrine, citing cases such as West Virginia v. EPA to point out that the Supreme Court remains highly skeptical of broad, unusual regulatory authority claimed through implicit delegations

Ultimately, the dissenters advocated for a return to the precedent established in the 1711 common law case Mitchel v. Reynolds, which highlighted the importance of evaluating non-competes on a case-by-case basis rather than issuing a sweeping ban

The Ryan and Properties of the Villages Litigation The defining death knell for the rule occurred in the United States District Court for the Northern District of Texas in the landmark litigation Ryan, LLC v. FTC
In August 2024, Judge Ada E. Brown ruled that the FTC fundamentally lacked the statutory authority to promulgate the rule, deeming it arbitrary and capricious
Consequently, the court issued a nationwide vacatur and injunction, halting the rule's implementation entirely

Simultaneously, in Properties of the Villages v. FTC, a federal court in Florida issued a narrower, plaintiff-specific injunction against the rule, relying heavily on the major questions doctrine to find that the agency exceeded its authority

Accession to Vacatur On September 5, 2025, the FTC formally withdrew its notice of appeal in the Fifth Circuit (Ryan, LLC v. FTC, No. 24-10951) and the Eleventh Circuit (Properties of the Villages v. FTC, No. 24-13102), officially abandoning the challenge to the district court rulings
The decision to abandon the appeal and accede to the vacatur was finalized by a 3-1 vote of the Commission
In their accompanying public statements, Chairman Ferguson and Commissioner Holyoak emphasized that the FTC lacked authority for a sweeping rule and that the rule's illegality was "patently obvious"
Conversely, Commissioner Rebecca Kelly Slaughter was the sole dissenting vote, issuing a statement arguing that abandoning the appeals severely undermined essential worker protections

The regulatory saga formally concluded when the FTC published a final rule in the Federal Register on February 12, 2026, officially removing the Non-Compete Rule from the Code of Federal Regulations, specifically 16 CFR part 910

A Return to Targeted Adjudication On September 4, 2025, the day before withdrawing its appeals, the FTC filed a complaint against Gateway Pet Memorial Services, alleging that the company's widespread use of one-year non-competes in the pet cremation industry constituted an anticompetitive practice violating Section 5 of the FTC Act
Under the proposed consent order, finalized on November 25, 2025, Gateway was barred from enforcing non-competes against approximately 1,800 workers

The order further forced the company to affirmatively notify employees that they were no longer bound by the agreements and imposed a strict 10-year compliance bar against entering into future non-competes with most employees

Business and Professions Code Section 16600 The bedrock of California's employment law is codified in California Business and Professions Code section 16600, which explicitly states that "every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void"

The statute recognizes exceptionally few exceptions, applying strictly to the sale of the goodwill of a business (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code Section 16601), the dissolution of a partnership (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code Section 16602), or the dissolution of a limited liability company (Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code Section 16602.5)

Edwards and AMN Healthcare The absolute nature of California's prohibition was decisively solidified by the California Supreme Court in the landmark case Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP, 44 Cal. 4th 937, decided on August 7, 2008

The California Supreme Court categorically rejected the "narrow restraint" exception previously utilized by the Ninth Circuit, ruling that Section 16600 represents a strict per se standard of invalidity in the employment context, without any regard to the "reasonableness" of the restraint

A decade later, the California Fourth District Court of Appeal drastically expanded this employee-friendly doctrine in AMN Healthcare, Inc. v. Aya Healthcare Servs., Inc., 28 Cal. App. 5th 923, decided in 2018

The court struck down the non-solicitation provision as void under Section 16600, holding that the clause impermissibly restrained the recruiters from engaging in their chosen profession of recruiting
This decision, later reinforced by cases like Barker v. Insight Global, LLC, essentially invalidated employee non-solicitation provisions throughout the state
SB 699 and AB 1076 Signed into law by Governor Gavin Newsom on September 1, 2023, and effective January 1, 2024, Senate Bill 699 added Section 16600.5 to the Business and Professions Code
First, it explicitly extends the prohibition extraterritorially, specifying that any contract void under Section 16600 is unenforceable "regardless of where and when the contract was signed"

Legislative findings accompanying the bill forcefully declared that "California's public policy against restraint of trade law trumps other state laws... regardless of the persons' state of residence"
It creates a private right of action permitting employees, former employees, and prospective employees to sue employers for injunctive relief, actual damages, or both
Signed into law on October 13, 2023, and also effective January 1, 2024, Assembly Bill 1076 amended Section 16600 and added Section 16600.1

Employers were legally mandated to send an individualized, written communication by February 14, 2024, to all current employees and former employees who were employed after January 1, 2022, explicitly notifying them that the non-compete provisions in their contracts were void
The notice had to be delivered to the last known address and the email address of the employee

Reed, Roberts and BDO Seidman The modern framework for assessing non-competes in New York was firmly established in Reed, Roberts Assoc. v. Strauman, 40 N.Y.2d 303, decided by the New York Court of Appeals in 1976
In this case, Reed Roberts Associates provided advice to employers regarding unemployment laws and had over 6,000 customers
Reed, Roberts established the definitive four-prong "Reasonableness Framework"
This standard was further refined in the 1999 landmark decision BDO Seidman v. Hirshberg, 93 N.Y.2d 382
Crucially, BDO Seidman firmly entrenched the precedent for "blue-penciling" or partial enforcement in New York

Rather than voiding the entire agreement as the lower appellate division had done, the court severed the invalid portions, enforcing an 18-month restriction solely to protect the specific client relationships the accountant had acquired and developed through his employment with BDO Seidman
3.3 The 2023–2026 Legislative Gridlock On June 20, 2023, the New York State Legislature passed Senate Bill S3100, a sweeping legislative overhaul intended to mimic California's absolute prohibition
Following intense lobbying from Wall Street and the financial sector, Governor Kathy Hochul vetoed the bill on December 22, 2023
In a targeted response to the governor's veto, Senator Sean Ryan introduced a revised bill, S4641, on February 10, 2025

This compromised legislation applied only prospectively and specifically exempted "highly compensated individuals" whose average annualized rate of cash compensation during the past three years was $500,000 or more
Despite passing the Senate on June 9, 2025, S4641 died in the Assembly Labor Committee before the legislative session ended
The legislation was resurrected on April 6, 2026, when Senator Michael Gianaris re-introduced the substantively identical text as Senate Bill S9759

Business and Commerce Code Section 15.50(a) The enforceability of general non-compete agreements in Texas is governed exclusively by the Texas Free Enterprise and Antitrust Act of 1983, specifically codified at Texas Business & Commerce Code Section 15.50(a)
First, the covenant not to compete must be "ancillary to or part of an otherwise enforceable agreement at the time the agreement is made"
Alex Sheshunoff and Marsh USA Historically, under the 1994 case Light v. Centel Cellular Co. of Tex., 883 S.W. 2d 642, the Texas Supreme Court utilized a highly restrictive standard
However, in the seminal 2006 case Alex Sheshunoff Management Services, L.P. v. Johnson, 209 S.W.3d 644, the Texas Supreme Court substantially relaxed this rigid interpretation
This was further expanded in 2009 by Mann Frankfort Stein & Lipp Advisors, Inc. v. Fielding, 289 S.W.3d 844, which allowed for implied promises of confidential information to satisfy the statute
The nature of valid consideration was further revolutionized in 2011 by Marsh USA Inc. v. Cook, 354 S.W.3d 764
The Texas Supreme Court ruled for the first time that the award of stock options to key employees serves as proper and sufficient consideration to support a non-compete

Crucially, however, despite the liberalization in Marsh, subsequent Texas jurisprudence firmly maintains that a pure financial payment—such as a cash bonus, a salary raise, or a severance payout—is not sufficient consideration to support a restrictive covenant in Texas
Senate Bill 1318 On June 20, 2025, Governor Greg Abbott signed Senate Bill 1318 into law, imposing sweeping, hardline restrictions on healthcare covenants effective September 1, 2025
SB 1318 amends the existing physician regulations under Section 15.50(b) and adds a completely new Section 15.501, establishing extreme structural limits on enforcement
The restricted area cannot exceed a five-mile radius from the specific location where the practitioner primarily practiced prior to the termination of their contract

Replaces the previous "reasonable price" arbitration standard with a strict statutory cap: the buyout amount cannot be greater than the practitioner's total annual salary and wages at the time of termination
Under Section 15.50(d), a covenant is entirely void and unenforceable if the physician is involuntarily discharged without "good cause"

Comparative Cross-Jurisdictional Analysis The collapse of the Federal Trade Commission's national rulemaking experiment in early 2026 created a massive regulatory vacuum, forcing the structural evolution of non-compete enforcement permanently back into the hands of state legislatures and local judiciaries
California's aggressive codification of extraterritorial application under SB 699 creates profound operational risks
2025's SB 1318 implemented rigid caps (1-year duration, 5-mile radius) and salary-based buyout limits for healthcare providers

The Doctrine of Qualified Immunity in Section 1983 Litigation (Gemini DR) The contemporary framework was forged in Harlow v. Fitzgerald, 457 U.S. 800 (1982), an 8-1 decision authored by Justice Lewis Powell, with Chief Justice Warren Burger authoring the sole dissent.
The case centered on A. Ernest Fitzgerald, a management analyst for the United States Air Force dismissed after testifying about cost overruns in the C-5A transport plane.
The aides moved for summary judgment claiming absolute and qualified immunity.
The Court held that "bare allegations of malice should not suffice to subject government officials either to the costs of trial or to the burdens of broad-reaching discovery."
Saucier v. Katz, 533 U.S. 194 (2001), mandated a rigid two-step sequence for adjudicating qualified immunity defenses.
The case involved animal rights protester Elliot Katz, who filed a Bivens action against military police officer Donald Saucier.
The Ninth Circuit had denied Saucier's motion for summary judgment.
The majority opinion was authored by Justice Anthony Kennedy.
Pearson v. Callahan, 555 U.S. 223 (2009).
Police officers had entered a suspect's home without a warrant relying on the "consent-once-removed" doctrine.
The Court held that the two-step sequence should no longer be regarded as mandatory.
Hope v. Pelzer, 536 U.S. 730 (2002).
Larry Hope was handcuffed to a stationary hitching post in the sun for seven hours.
The Court held that "general statements of the law... may apply with obvious clarity to the specific conduct in question."
Taylor v. Riojas, 141 S. Ct. 52 (2020), a per curiam decision.
The Court reversed a Fifth Circuit grant of immunity to officials who confined an inmate in a cell covered in feces for six days.
The Court held the conduct was so egregious that any reasonable officer should have realized it offended the Eighth Amendment.
McCoy v. Alamu, 141 S. Ct. 1364 (2021), summarily vacated a Fifth Circuit decision granting immunity to a correctional officer who deployed pepper spray into an inmate's face.
City of Tahlequah v. Bond, 142 S. Ct. 9 (2021), and Rivas-Villegas v. Cortesluna, 142 S. Ct. 4 (2021), reversed appellate decisions denying immunity.
In Rivas-Villegas, the Supreme Court held the prior case law was "materially distinguishable."
In Ramirez v. Guadarrama, 3 F.4th 129 (5th Cir. 2021), Arlington police tased a suicidal man holding a gas can, causing him to burst into flames.
The Supreme Court denied certiorari.
In Zorn v. Linton (2025), the incident stemmed from the January 8, 2015 inauguration of Governor Peter Shumlin at the Vermont state capitol.
Sergeant Jacob Zorn applied a "wristlock" maneuver to Shela Linton.
The Supreme Court reversed in a per curiam opinion.
Justices Sotomayor, Kagan, and Jackson issued a dissent.
In Smith v. Scott (2026), officers utilized a bodyweight compression technique on a hallucinating schizophrenic man.
The Supreme Court summarily vacated the Ninth Circuit's judgment and remanded in light of Zorn v. Linton.
Nieves v. Bartlett, 587 U.S. 391 (2019), held that objective probable cause for an arrest generally defeats a First Amendment retaliatory arrest claim.
Gonzalez v. Trevino, 602 U.S. (2024).
Sylvia Gonzalez, a 72-year-old city councilwoman in Castle Hills, Texas, initiated a petition to remove the city manager.
The Supreme Court vacated the Fifth Circuit's judgment in a per curiam opinion.
Tolan v. Cotton, 572 U.S. 650 (2014).
Bellaire police Sergeant Jeffrey Cotton fired three bullets at Robert Tolan.
The Court ruled that a court must take all facts in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party.
Perttu v. Richards (June 18, 2025).
In a 5-4 decision authored by Chief Justice John Roberts, the Court affirmed the Sixth Circuit's judgment.
Justice Amy Coney Barrett authored a dissent.
The New Mexico Civil Rights Act (2021) caps damages at $2 million per claim.
New York City Council passed a local ordinance in 2021 eliminating the qualified immunity defense for NYPD officers.
In 2022, the Nevada Supreme Court ruled in Mack v. Williams that federal qualified immunity would not apply to state-level actions.
The California Supreme Court ruled in Leon v. County of Riverside (2023).
The Ohio ballot initiative targets placement on the November 3, 2026 ballot.
) On April 22, 2025, the full Supreme Court lifted the stay over the dissents of Justices Kavanaugh, Thomas, and Alito.

An Exhaustive Legal Analysis of the Fair Use Doctrine (Gemini DR) The intellectual property regime of the United States is fundamentally rooted in the U.S. Constitution, which grants Congress the power to promote the progress of science and useful arts.
The basic architectural framework for the current law was established by the comprehensive Copyright Act of 1976.
Enacted into law on October 19, 1976, as Public Law 94-553 (90 Stat. 2546), this legislation codified the common-law doctrine of fair use into 17 U.S.C. Section 107.
The statute has been subject to subsequent amendments, including Public Law 101-650 on December 1, 1990, and Public Law 102-492 on October 24, 1992.

Section 107 explicitly declares that the fair use of a copyrighted work is not an infringement of copyright if the work is utilized for purposes such as criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching, scholarship, or research.
The statute clarifies that teaching purposes can explicitly include the creation of multiple copies for classroom use.
The first statutory factor requires courts to examine the purpose and character of the use, including whether such use is of a commercial nature or is for nonprofit educational purposes.
Transformative use examines whether the new work merely supersedes the objects of the original creation, or whether it adds new expression, meaning, or message.
The commercial nature of a secondary work does not automatically preclude a finding of fair use if the use is sufficiently transformative.
The second statutory factor assesses the nature of the copyrighted work itself.
Works that are highly creative are located closer to the core of intended copyright protection than works that are primarily factual or functional.
A secondary use may fail the third factor even if it appropriates only a tiny percentage of the original, provided the copied portion constitutes the qualitative "heart" of the original.
The fourth factor analyzes the effect of the secondary use upon the potential market for, or value of, the copyrighted work.
Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc., 510 U.S. 569, was decided on March 7, 1994.
The District Court initially granted summary judgment in favor of 2 Live Crew.
The Supreme Court unanimously reversed the Sixth Circuit.
Following remand, the parties settled out of court.
Google LLC v. Oracle America, Inc., 593 U.S. 1, decided on April 5, 2021.
Google copied roughly 11,500 lines of code from the Java SE program.
The copied lines constituted only about 0.4 percent of the entire Java SE program.
Justice Clarence Thomas filed a dissenting opinion.
Justice Amy Coney Barrett took no part in the consideration or decision of the case.
Andy Warhol Foundation v. Goldsmith, 143 S. Ct. 1258, decided on May 18, 2023.
In 1984, Goldsmith's agency licensed a photograph to Vanity Fair for use as an "artist reference."
The district court initially granted summary judgment for AWF.
The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit reversed.
Thomson Reuters Enterprise Centre GmbH v. ROSS Intelligence Inc., decided on February 11, 2025.
Judge Bibas found that ROSS had directly infringed 2,243 Westlaw headnotes.
The court concluded ROSS's use was not transformative.
Bartz v. Anthropic PBC, decided by Judge William Alsup on June 23, 2025.
Anthropic had utilized a dataset containing over seven million pirated works.
The court certified the class action for the piracy claims, defining the class to encompass 482,460 distinct books.
The total settlement fund was $1.5 billion paid by Anthropic.
The settlement included 243,397 unique authors and 15,786 unique publishers.
Kadrey v. Meta Platforms, Inc., decided June 25, 2025.
Judge Chhabria denied the plaintiffs' motion and granted Meta's cross-motion.
On October 27, 2025, Judge Sidney Stein denied OpenAI's motion to dismiss the output-based copyright infringement claims.
OpenAI had intentionally deleted its "Books1" and "Books2" training datasets.
In August 2025, Judge William Orrick issued an order allowing the plaintiffs' core direct infringement claims to move forward.
A jury trial is scheduled for April 5, 2027.
On March 25, 2025, U.S. District Judge Eumi K. Lee denied the application for an interim injunction.
The court is scheduled to hear summary judgment motions on July 15, 2026.
Getty Images v. Stability AI Limited, handed down November 4, 2025 by the High Court of Justice in the UK.
Getty relied on 11 sample works to prove subsistence and ownership.
The U.S. Copyright Office Part 1 report was published on July 31, 2024.
Part 3 pre-publication version was released on May 9, 2025.
On March 20, 2026, the Trump Administration released its National AI Legislative Framework.
"Except as provided in this chapter, every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void."

As amended by AB 1076, § 16600(b)(1) now provides that the section "shall be read broadly, in accordance with Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP (2008) 44 Cal.4th 937, to void the application of any noncompete agreement in an employment context."
Section 16600(c) extends the prohibition to contracts where the person being restrained is not a party to the contract.
Section 16601 permits a non-compete on the sale of the goodwill of a business or of an owner's entire ownership interest.
Section 16602 permits a non-compete upon dissolution of or dissociation from a partnership.
Section 16602.5 permits a non-compete upon dissolution of, or termination of a member's interest in, a limited liability company.

The California Supreme Court confirmed in Edwards that "[n]oncompetition agreements are invalid under section 16600 in California even if narrowly drawn, unless they fall within the applicable statutory exceptions of sections 16601, 16602, or 16602.5."

Raymond Edwards II, a CPA hired as a tax manager by Arthur Andersen in Los Angeles, signed a non-compete barring him for 18 months after departure from performing professional services for any client on whose account he had worked during the prior 18 months.
The California Supreme Court held the agreement void under § 16600 and rejected the Ninth Circuit's "narrow restraint" exception.
The Court expressly declined to address the "so-called trade secret exception to section 16600."
SB 699 added Business and Professions Code § 16600.5, providing that any contract void under the chapter "is unenforceable regardless of where and when the contract was signed."
SB 699 also created a private right of action allowing employees, former employees, and prospective employees to sue for injunctive relief, actual damages, and attorney's fees.

AB 1076 codified Edwards in § 16600(b)(1) and added § 16600.1, requiring employers to notify, by February 14, 2024, current employees and former employees employed after January 1, 2022 that their non-compete clauses are void.
Failure to provide the notice is an act of unfair competition subject to civil penalties of up to $2,500 per violation.

In DraftKings Inc. v. Hermalyn, the First Circuit on September 26, 2024 affirmed a preliminary injunction enforcing a Massachusetts-law non-compete against a former DraftKings executive who moved to California to join Fanatics.
New York has no general statute governing or prohibiting employment non-competes; enforceability is governed by common-law caselaw applying a reasonableness standard.

The New York Court of Appeals articulated the "prevailing standard of reasonableness," holding that a restraint is reasonable only if it: (1) is no greater than required to protect the legitimate interest of the employer, (2) does not impose undue hardship on the employee, and (3) is not injurious to the public.
The full citation is BDO Seidman v. Hirshberg, 93 N.Y.2d 382, 690 N.Y.S.2d 854, 712 N.E.2d 1220 (1999).

The Court limited cognizable employer interests to protection against misappropriation of trade secrets or confidential customer lists, or protection from competition by an employee whose services are "unique or extraordinary."
The Court found the covenant overbroad as to clients Hirshberg never served, but applied partial enforcement to the portion covering clients he had served within an 18-month restriction.
The New York Legislature passed S3100A in June 2023, which would have banned nearly all non-compete agreements.

Governor Kathy Hochul vetoed the bill on December 22, 2023, stating in her veto memo that she had "long supported limits on non-compete agreements for middle-class and low-wage workers" but objected to the bill's broad scope.
News reports indicated Governor Hochul sought to limit the ban to individuals earning up to $250,000, while sponsors were agreeable to a $300,000 limit.

On February 10, 2025, Senator Sean Ryan introduced S4641, a narrower bill that would add Labor Law § 191-d, banning non-competes for "covered individuals" but exempting "highly compensated individuals" earning $500,000 or more annually.
The bill caps permissible non-competes at one year and requires payment of salary (garden leave) during the restriction.
S4641 passed the Senate on June 9, 2025 by a 40–22 vote and moved to the Assembly Labor Committee, where it had not advanced as of early 2026.
In April 2026, Senator Michael Gianaris reintroduced a substantively identical bill, S9759.

New York Labor Law § 202-k (the 2008 "Broadcast Employees Freedom to Work Act") prohibits broadcasting-industry employers from requiring broadcast employees to refrain from obtaining employment after the conclusion of employment.

A covenant not to compete is enforceable "if it is ancillary to or part of an otherwise enforceable agreement at the time the agreement is made to the extent that it contains limitations as to time, geographical area, and scope of activity to be restrained that are reasonable."
Section 15.52 makes the statutory criteria exclusive, preempting common-law and other bases.
Courts first determine whether there is an "otherwise enforceable agreement," then whether the covenant is "ancillary to or part of" that agreement.
Texas is one of the few states where judges reform (rather than void) overbroad covenants under § 15.51(c).

The Texas Supreme Court held that a unilateral contract can satisfy the Act: a covenant becomes enforceable when the employer performs its promise, even if that promise was illusory when made, modifying the Court's 1994 decision in Light v. Centel Cellular Co.

The Court held that consideration need not "give rise to" the employer's interest in restraining competition; it need only be "reasonably related to" an interest worthy of protection, such as goodwill.
The Court held that stock options granted to a managing director were reasonably related to Marsh's interest in protecting goodwill.
Signed by Governor Greg Abbott on June 20, 2025, SB 1318 amends §§ 15.50 and 15.52 and adds § 15.501.

For physician non-competes, it requires a buyout capped at the physician's total annual salary and wages at termination, expiration no later than one year after termination, and a geographic limit of no more than a five-mile radius from the physician's primary practice location.
It also makes a physician non-compete void and unenforceable if the physician is involuntarily discharged without "good cause."
New § 15.501 extends the buyout cap, one-year duration limit, and five-mile geographic limit to dentists, nurses, and physician assistants.
The law applies only to agreements entered into or renewed on or after September 1, 2025.

On April 23, 2024, the FTC voted 3–2 to issue the Non-Compete Clause Rule (16 CFR Part 910), declaring it an unfair method of competition under Section 5 of the FTC Act to enter into or enforce non-competes with workers.

It banned all new non-competes and rendered existing non-competes unenforceable after the effective date — except that existing non-competes with "senior executives" (defined as workers in a policy-making position who received compensation of at least $151,164 in the preceding year) could remain in force.
The FTC stated that "[a]n estimated 30 million workers—nearly one in five Americans—are subject to a noncompete."
The FTC also projected that the rule would foster "more than 8,500 new startups that would be created a year once noncompetes are banned."
The rule was published in the Federal Register on May 7, 2024 (89 FR 38342), with an effective date of September 4, 2024.

Litigation — Ryan LLC v. FTC. On August 20, 2024, U.S. District Judge Ada Brown granted summary judgment to the plaintiffs in Ryan LLC v. FTC, No. 3:24-cv-00986, holding that the FTC lacks statutory authority to promulgate substantive unfair-methods-of-competition rules.
Judge Brown wrote that "[t]he FTC lacks substantive rulemaking authority with respect to unfair methods of competition."
She held the ruling has "nationwide effect," setting aside the rule so it "shall not be enforced or otherwise take effect on September 4, 2024, or thereafter."

Litigation — ATS Tree Services v. FTC. On July 23, 2024, U.S. District Judge Kelley Brisbon Hodge denied ATS Tree Services' motion to stay the effective date and preliminarily enjoin the rule, holding that the FTC acted within its authority under the FTC Act.
ATS voluntarily dismissed its case on October 4, 2024.
In Properties of the Villages, Inc. v. FTC, Judge Timothy Corrigan granted a preliminary injunction (limited to the named plaintiff) on August 14, 2024, invoking the major questions doctrine.
On October 18, 2024, the FTC filed a notice of appeal of the Ryan ruling to the Fifth Circuit (No. 24-10951).
On September 5, 2025, the FTC voted 3–1 to dismiss both appeals and accede to the vacatur of the Non-Compete Rule.

Formal removal from the CFR. The FTC published a final rule in the Federal Register, effective February 12, 2026, formally removing the Non-Compete Rule (16 CFR Part 910) from the Code of Federal Regulations.

In a 2025 action against Gateway Services, a pet cremation company, the FTC announced on September 5, 2025 a proposed consent order that "will free nearly 1,800 employees from these restrictive agreements," and finalized the consent order on November 25, 2025 by a 2–0 vote.

The Current Doctrine of Qualified Immunity for Police Officers in 42 U.S.C. § 1983 Cases Details Qualified immunity shields police officers sued under 42 U.S.C. § 1983 from damages unless they violated "clearly established" law — a two-prong test under which courts may decide either prong first, and the right must be defined with great specificity.
42 U.S.C. § 1983 makes "[e]very person" who, under color of state law, deprives another of constitutional rights "liable to the party injured" — it contains no text creating any immunity.
The modern "clearly established law" standard was created in Harlow v. Fitzgerald (1982), replacing the older subjective good-faith test with a purely objective one.
Courts require the plaintiff to identify a prior case — typically on closely analogous facts — placing the constitutional question "beyond debate."
A right is clearly established only when it is "sufficiently clear that every reasonable official would have understood that what he is doing violates that right."
The Court draws this from Mullenix v. Luna, 577 U.S. 7 (2015).
The Court has described the doctrine as protecting "all but the plainly incompetent or those who knowingly violate the law" (Malley v. Briggs).

The Court has "repeatedly told courts — and the Ninth Circuit in particular — not to define clearly established law at a high level of generality," drawing on Ashcroft v. al-Kidd, 563 U.S. 731 (2011).
This requirement traces to Anderson v. Creighton, 483 U.S. 635 (1987).
The relevant precedent must define the right with a "high degree of specificity" (District of Columbia v. Wesby, 583 U.S. 48 (2018)).

arlow v. Fitzgerald, 457 U.S. 800 (1982), decided 8-1 (Justice Powell writing; Chief Justice Burger dissenting), held that "government officials performing discretionary functions generally are shielded from liability for civil damages insofar as their conduct does not violate clearly established statutory or constitutional rights of which a reasonable person would have known."
It abandoned the prior subjective "good faith" inquiry in favor of "objective legal reasonableness."
Justice Scalia, writing for the Court, established that "the contours of the right must be sufficiently clear that a reasonable official would understand that what he is doing violates that right."

Saucier v. Katz, 533 U.S. 194 (2001), decided June 18, 2001, held that the qualified immunity inquiry is "not susceptible of fusion with the question whether unreasonable force was used in making the arrest" and mandated a rigid two-step sequence.

In a 6-3 decision (Justice Stevens writing), the Court denied immunity to Alabama guards who handcuffed inmate Larry Hope to a "hitching post" in the sun for seven hours, holding officials "can be on notice that their conduct violates established law even in novel factual circumstances."

Justice Alito, writing for a unanimous Court, made the Saucier sequence discretionary rather than mandatory, holding judges "should be permitted to exercise their sound discretion in deciding which of the two prongs of the qualified immunity analysis should be addressed first."

In a per curiam decision on November 2, 2020, the Court reversed the Fifth Circuit's grant of immunity to officers who confined inmate Trent Taylor for six days in cells covered "nearly floor to ceiling" in feces and then raw sewage.
It was the first time the Court relied on the obviousness of a violation to overturn a grant of qualified immunity.

On a GVR order (February 2021), the Court vacated the Fifth Circuit's grant of immunity to a guard who pepper-sprayed inmate Prince McCoy in the face, remanding for reconsideration in light of Taylor v. Riojas.

In a unanimous per curiam decision on October 18, 2021, the Court reversed the Ninth Circuit and granted immunity to a Union City officer who briefly placed his knee on the back of an armed suspect, finding the sole cited precedent "materially distinguishable."

In a unanimous per curiam decision the same day, the Court granted immunity to officers who fatally shot Dominic Rollice as he raised a hammer, holding "the officers plainly did not violate any clearly established law."

Egbert v. Boule, 596 U.S. 482 (2022), decided June 8, 2022 by 6-3 (Justice Thomas writing), held that no Bivens damages remedy extends to Fourth Amendment excessive-force or First Amendment retaliation claims against federal agents.

Barnes v. Felix, 605 U.S. 73 (2025), decided May 15, 2025, in a unanimous opinion by Justice Kagan, rejected the Fifth Circuit's "moment-of-threat" rule, holding reasonableness must be judged on the "totality of the circumstances."

In a 6-3 per curiam decision, the Court reversed the Second Circuit and granted immunity to Vermont Sergeant Jacob Zorn, holding the lower court failed to "identify a case where an officer taking similar actions in similar circumstances 'was held to have violated' the Constitution."
Mullenix v. Luna, 577 U.S. 7 (2015) (officer who fatally shot a fleeing driver from an overpass granted immunity).

The Fair Use Doctrine in U.S. Copyright Law (Claude DR) Section 107 lists six favored example purposes in its preamble (criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching, scholarship, research) and four factors: purpose/character, nature of the work, amount/substantiality used, and market effect.
Transformative use originated in Judge Pierre Leval's 1990 Harvard Law Review article and was adopted by the Supreme Court in Campbell (1994).
Google v. Oracle (2021) found fair use for copying ~11,500 lines of Java API declaring code (0.4% of the program), assuming copyrightability without deciding it.

Warhol v. Goldsmith (2023, 7–2) held the first factor disfavored the Warhol Foundation because its commercial licensing of "Orange Prince" shared substantially the same purpose as Goldsmith's photograph.
Fair use is codified at Section 107 of the Copyright Act of 1976 (Pub. L. 94-553, enacted Oct. 19, 1976).

The statute provides that "the fair use of a copyrighted work … for purposes such as criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching (including multiple copies for classroom use), scholarship, or research, is not an infringement of copyright."
The six illustrative favored purposes are criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching, scholarship, and research.
Congress intended Section 107 to "restate the present judicial doctrine of fair use, not to change, narrow, or enlarge it in any way," describing fair use as "an equitable rule of reason."
The Supreme Court in Harper & Row v. Nation Enterprises (1985) called the fourth factor "undoubtedly the single most important element of fair use."
Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc., 510 U.S. 569 (1994), decided March 7, 1994, a unanimous decision by Justice Souter, held that a commercial parody can be fair use.
The Court asked "whether and to what extent the new work is 'transformative'" — whether it "adds something new, with a further purpose or different character."
The Court stated "the more transformative the new work, the less will be the significance of other factors, like commercialism."
The transformative-use concept derived from Judge Leval's 1990 article "Toward a Fair Use Standard," 103 Harv. L. Rev. 1105.

Google LLC v. Oracle America, Inc., 593 U.S. 1 (2021), decided April 5, 2021, in a 6–2 opinion by Justice Breyer, held that Google's copying of approximately 11,500 lines of declaring code was fair use as a matter of law.
The 11,500 lines were just 0.4% of the entire 2.86-million-line Java SE program.

Andy Warhol Foundation v. Goldsmith, 598 U.S. 508 (2023), decided May 18, 2023, in a 7–2 opinion by Justice Sotomayor, held that the first fair use factor did not favor the Warhol Foundation's 2016 commercial licensing of "Orange Prince" to Condé Nast.
The Court clarified that Campbell "cannot be read to mean that the first factor weighs in favor of any use that adds some new expression, meaning or message."

Professor Barton Beebe's empirical study found that of the core opinions in which factor one favored fair use, 92.2% ultimately found fair use, while of those in which factor one disfavored fair use, 96.6% found no fair use.
The U.S. Copyright Office, Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 3 (May 9, 2025), concluded AI training is not categorically fair use.

The report warned that "making commercial use of vast troves of copyrighted works to produce expressive content that competes with them in existing markets … goes beyond established fair use boundaries."
Judge Stephanos Bibas granted partial summary judgment for Thomson Reuters, holding Ross's copying of Westlaw headnotes to train its AI legal-research tool was not fair use.
The court found Ross copied at least 2,243 headnotes.
Judge William Alsup held Anthropic's use of books to train its Claude LLMs was "exceedingly transformative" and fair use, but downloading pirated books was not.
Anthropic agreed to pay a minimum of $1.5 billion into a settlement fund.
